title: Law Review Cite-Checking: Verifying That a Source Actually Supports the Proposition

extracted.subtask_short: Verifying every footnote supports its claim pre-publication
extracted.subtask_description: Describes the formal, mandatory pre-publication procedure by which law journal student editors verify that every cited source actually supports the sentence it's attached to, distinct from formatting/style verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four-part quality standard: accurate / valid / non-plagiarized / useful
rubrics_metrics.description: Accurate - 'the citation content and format leads the reader to the correct source.' Valid - 'the source actually supports the author's claim/statement' (the core claim-matching criterion). Non-plagiarized - every proposition in the text receives proper attribution. Useful - the citation 'provides value to the reader,' i.e., is not a superfluous or decorative citation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A citation can be 'accurate' (correctly leads to the right source) while being 'invalid' (the source doesn't actually say what's claimed) - a claim-matching metric could report these as four separate axes rather than one composite score.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive verification vs formatting verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Cite-checking is 'a method of verifying an author's statements are adequately supported by other sources and the citation conforms to the appropriate style guide.' Two distinct jobs are bundled: (1) substantive verification - does the source actually support the claim, and (2) formatting verification - is the citation itself correctly styled. Verification is not satisfied merely by confirming the source exists and is correctly formatted; the checker must locate the specific passage and confirm it says what the author claims it says.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is a citation needed (threshold necessity check)
rubrics_metrics.description: A threshold/necessity check before verification even begins: is this actually a claim requiring source support (e.g., a factual/empirical assertion rather than the author's own original argument)?

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the cited authority support the statement made in the text
rubrics_metrics.description: The core claim-matching verification question, applied to every footnote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introductory signal must match the true strength of support
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Are the introductory signals and parentheticals appropriate according to Bluebook Rule 1?' Given that the source does or doesn't directly/indirectly/analogically support the claim, has the author selected the correct signal (no signal / See / Cf. / But see / etc.) to represent the true strength of that support?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This step effectively re-uses the graded support-signal taxonomy as a checkable output of the verification process, not just an input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bidirectional claim-source match check
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Do the claims presented in the article match the claims made in or about the cited source?' - phrased as a bidirectional match check (the citing text's characterization of the source, and the source's actual content, must correspond), plus confirm the version cited is the most current/authoritative available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pincite to the exact supporting location
rubrics_metrics.description: Pincite to the exact location (page number, statute section, etc.) within the source that supports the specific proposition - a citation to an entire 40-page article without a pincite to the actually-relevant page is treated as inadequate, since it doesn't let a reader (or a downstream auditor) efficiently verify the specific supporting passage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A citation without a pincite/specific location pointer should be treated as harder-to-verify / lower-confidence by default - 'cites the whole source' is weaker evidence of true support than 'cites the specific page/section,' directly paralleling the evidence-sentence retrieval bottleneck found in the biomedical NLP annotation-scheme literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify against the final published version of the source
rubrics_metrics.description: Checkers must use 'the final, publisher's version with enough information to create relevant pincites' (i.e., not a preprint or draft version that might differ from what's actually cited, and not a version lacking page/section granularity needed to point to the exact supporting passage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim can be 'supported' by a preprint that changed before final publication, which downstream automated matching against only the final version would incorrectly flag as unsupported, or vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Escalate ambiguous or hard-to-locate sources rather than partial-verify
rubrics_metrics.description: If a source is ambiguous or hard to locate, escalate (consult a reference librarian, dictionary of legal abbreviations, alternative search) rather than approving on partial verification.
